clinicalPearls: An occupational disorder caused by prolonged use of hand-held vibrating tools, with vascular, neurological and musculoskeletal components
The vascular component is an episodic cold-induced blanching of the fingers, a secondary form of Raynaud phenomenon (vibration white finger)
The neurological component causes numbness, tingling and reduced dexterity and fine sensation
Symptoms are graded by severity using recognised occupational staging scales
It is an important prescribed or reportable occupational disease in many jurisdictions
Management centres on reducing vibration exposure, keeping warm and stopping smoking, as symptoms may not fully reverse
reference.pathophysiology: Repeated transmission of vibration from hand-held tools injures the digital vasculature and peripheral nerves. Vascular injury and abnormal sympathetic responses produce exaggerated cold-induced vasospasm and blanching of the fingers, while damage to peripheral nerve fibres and mechanoreceptors causes sensory loss and impaired dexterity. Chronic exposure also affects muscles, joints and bone. The changes reflect cumulative dose, so risk rises with the intensity and duration of vibration exposure.
additionalDifferentials: Secondary Raynaud from connective tissue disease
Carpal tunnel syndrome or other entrapment neuropathy
additionalInvestigations: Detailed occupational history quantifying vibration exposure
Assessment and staging of vascular and sensorineural components
Cold provocation and vascular testing where available
Nerve conduction studies to assess or exclude entrapment neuropathy
Exclusion of connective tissue disease causing secondary Raynaud
redFlags: Features suggesting an underlying connective tissue disease
Rapidly progressive sensory or motor deficit
Asymmetric or unilateral vascular signs suggesting another cause
reference.prognosis: Early vascular changes may improve if exposure stops, but established neurological damage often persists; continued exposure leads to progression and greater disability.
pitfalls: Failing to take a quantified occupational vibration history
Attributing symptoms solely to carpal tunnel syndrome
Missing an underlying connective tissue disease
Not advising exposure reduction and smoking cessation
